Tsar Alexander II. On March 13, 1881, the Tsar Liberator was mortally wounded by a bomb thrown by members of the revolutionary group Narodnaya Volya, or People's Will, in Saint Petersburg.

The assassination was shocking because it demonstrated that even cautious reform could not appease radical revolutionaries. Alexander was mortally wounded and died within hours at the Winter Palace from blast injuries. Narodnaya Volya had attempted to assassinate Alexander II multiple times over the years, but this bombing succeeded after years of failed attempts.

Alexander II had earned the epithet "Liberator" by freeing the serfs in 1861, one of the most significant reforms in Russian history. Yet by the 1870s, he had become increasingly conservative and repressive. The revolutionaries rejected his reforms as inadequate and demanded the overthrow of the entire system. Narodnaya Volya's ideology blended anarchism, socialism, and Russian nihilism. They believed terrorism was justified as a tool against autocracy.

Alexander's son, Alexander III, became tsar and immediately adopted a policy of strict reaction and repression. The executive of Narodnaya Volya, including the female terrorist Sophia Perovskaya, were arrested and executed. Alexander III blamed liberalism itself for the assassination and reversed his father's reforms, leading to decades of autocratic rule.

The assassination of Alexander II exemplifies the paradox of revolutionary violence: by killing a reformer, the terrorists provoked a crackdown far harsher than anything they opposed. The event marks a critical moment in Russian history—the point at which the Romanov autocracy chose reaction over evolution, a choice that would contribute to the instability leading to revolution in 1917. Alexander II's death also stands as a watershed in the history of anarchist and socialist ideology. Was terrorism a justified weapon against autocracy, or did it discredit the cause? Russian intellectuals debated this question for decades. The event discredited radical terrorism in Russian intellectual circles for a generation but also radicalized the next wave of revolutionaries.
